summary: Terazosin is a long-acting selective alpha-1 adrenergic blocker used for symptomatic benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and for hypertension. In BPH it relaxes smooth muscle in the bladder neck and prostate to improve urinary flow and symptoms; in hypertension it lowers peripheral vascular resistance. It must be started at 1 mg at bedtime because of a marked first-dose hypotensive/syncopal effect. Common effects are dizziness, asthenia, nasal congestion and postural hypotension; it can also cause intraoperative floppy iris syndrome at cataract surgery.
indications: Treatment of symptomatic benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)
Treatment of hypertension, alone or with other antihypertensive agents

dosage.d: Initial 1 mg at bedtime; titrate stepwise to 2, 5, then 10 mg once daily
dosage.n: 10 mg/day usually needed; assess after 4-6 weeks; some need 20 mg

dosage.d: Initial 1 mg at bedtime; usual range 1-5 mg once daily (up to 20 mg)
dosage.n: Adjust dose and 12 vs 24 h interval to BP response

dosage.d: Reinstitute using the initial 1 mg bedtime regimen
dosage.n: First-dose effect recurs if therapy lapses several days
Renal impairment does not significantly alter elimination

admin: Give the FIRST dose (1 mg) at bedtime to reduce the risk of first-dose syncope
Never start with the 2, 5 or 10 mg strengths
Titrate the dose slowly; add other antihypertensives with caution
Advise the patient to avoid driving or hazardous tasks for 12 hours after the first dose, after a dose increase, or after restarting therapy
In suspected BPH, rule out prostate carcinoma before starting; tell the ophthalmologist before cataract surgery
moa: Terazosin selectively blocks postsynaptic alpha-1 adrenoceptors. In BPH it relaxes smooth muscle in the bladder neck, prostatic capsule and prostate (the dynamic component of outlet obstruction), improving urine flow and symptoms without affecting bladder contractility. In hypertension, alpha-1 blockade in vascular smooth muscle reduces peripheral resistance and lowers blood pressure.

relative: Concurrent verapamil or other antihypertensives (additive hypotension)
Planned cataract surgery (intraoperative floppy iris syndrome)
monitor: Blood pressure supine and standing, especially at initiation
Prostate evaluation (rule out carcinoma) before therapy

preg: Pregnancy Category C. Animal studies showed fetal effects largely secondary to maternal toxicity at high doses; there are no adequate, well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Not recommended during pregnancy unless the potential benefit justifies the potential risk.
lact: It is not known whether terazosin is excreted in human milk. Because many drugs are excreted in breast milk, use caution when administering to a nursing woman.
renal: No dosage adjustment is necessary; impaired renal function does not significantly affect terazosin elimination, and the small amount removed by hemodialysis does not require supplementation.
hepatic: Terazosin is cleared mainly by hepatic/biliary metabolism with minimal first-pass effect; use caution in hepatic impairment, though no specific dose adjustment is defined in the label.

major: PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil) - additive hypotension
Verapamil and other antihypertensives - significant additive blood-pressure lowering; may require dose reduction/retitration
moderate: Diuretics/beta-blockers - additive BP effects (generally well tolerated)
minor: NSAIDs - may modestly blunt antihypertensive effect
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; food delays the peak by about 40 minutes but does not meaningfully reduce absorption.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid or limit alcohol; it worsens orthostatic hypotension, dizziness and the risk of syncope.
interactions.diagnostics: Small decreases in hematocrit, hemoglobin, WBC, total protein and albumin (likely hemodilution) may be seen; no significant effect on PSA.

serious: Syncope, especially with the first dose
Intraoperative floppy iris syndrome during cataract surgery
emergency: Prolonged painful erection (priapism) requiring urgent care

monitoring: Blood pressure (supine and standing), particularly during initiation and titration
Symptoms of orthostatic hypotension or syncope
Periodic assessment of urinary symptoms/flow in BPH
Prostate examination to exclude carcinoma before starting
counsel: Take the first dose at bedtime; you may feel dizzy or faint when you stand - get up slowly
Avoid driving or operating machinery for 12 hours after the first dose, a dose increase, or restarting
If you stop the medicine for a few days, you must restart at the low bedtime dose - do not jump back to your old dose
Sit or lie down if you feel dizzy or faint; report bothersome dizziness or palpitations
Tell your eye surgeon you take this drug before any cataract surgery; seek urgent care for a prolonged painful erection
pk: Blood pressure/symptom effect within hours; full BPH response over 4-6 weeks
Store at 20-25 C; protect from light and moisture; tight container
pearls: Classic first-dose phenomenon: always start 1 mg at bedtime and re-titrate after any interruption
In BPH it relieves the dynamic (smooth-muscle) component - prostate size does not predict symptom severity
Alpha-blockers cause intraoperative floppy iris syndrome - warn the cataract surgeon in advance
No renal dose adjustment and only ~10% removed by dialysis
Rule out prostate cancer before attributing symptoms to BPH
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as you remember unless it is nearly time for the next dose - then skip it and resume your schedule; do not double up. If you have missed several days, contact your prescriber, as you may need to restart at the low bedtime dose.
overdose: Overdose chiefly causes hypotension. Support the cardiovascular system: keep the patient supine to restore blood pressure and heart rate; if inadequate, give volume expanders, then vasopressors as needed, and monitor/support renal function. Terazosin is 90-94% protein bound, so dialysis is unlikely to help.
